newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers vow to tighten road/rail blockade.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers vow to tighten road/rail blockade.

text.p: Greece's defiant farmers vowed to tighten their eight-day blockade of the nation's road and rail links on Thursday after talks with the ruling socialists failed amid boos and jeers.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis, facing his first crisis since winning September elections, hastily arranged meetings with the biggest unions on Thursday to try to prevent the farmers' revolt from spreading to other sectors of the economy.
He met the General Confederation of Greek Workers (GSEE), the biggest labour grouping which staged a one-day nationwide strike last week and has threatened more action.
He will meet the civil servants union (ADEDY) later in the day. ADEDY joined the nationwide strike and helped to bring the country's vast public sector to a standstill.
Greece has been hit by a wave of work stoppages since Simitis submitted his 1997 budget, calling for sacrifices by all so that targets for economic convergence with EU partners would be met.
But the farmers' uprising is his main headache, bringing all overland commercial transport to a halt, dealing a blow to the economy and raising fears of soaring prices fueling inflation.
A cabinet meeting chaired by Simitis on Wednesday rejected anything more than minor concessions, saying farmers' demands would cost some two trillion drachmas ($8 billion).
The farmers want better price supports, cheaper fuel, the rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts and lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on farmer equipment.
Simitis dispatched Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas to the farmers' Larissa heaquarters in Thessaly to deliver the stern message. He was greeted by an avalanche of boos and jeers.
"The talks were fruitless. The agriculture minister repeated the government's known positions which don't satisfy us," a farmers' representative told reporters late on Wednesday.
An army of more than 10,000 tractors has fanned out across Greece, seizing toll booths and blockading road and rail links. Sprawling tent cities line the roads.

After Tzoumakas left empty handed, the farmers threatened to extend their crippling blockade to the Corinth bridge, linking Athens to the fertile southern Peloponnese peninsula as well as to close the Albanian border and other key points.
Farmers have closed traffic at the Bulgarian and Turkish borders, and put up more than 40 barricades at key intersections throughout the country.

The blockade began last Thursday, when the farmers closed main national road and rail links between Athens and Salonika. It has now left hundreds of international and domestic lorries stranded at the roadside.
Food merchants said stocks remain high, and prices largely under control, but have warned customers that should the protest continue next week there will be real problems.
